newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian conservatives revive tax reform push.
newsitem.headline: Australian conservatives revive tax reform push.

text.p: Australia's conservative coalition government threw itself into a campaign for tax reform on Wednesday, reviving the controversy that cost it a seemingly unloseable election in 1993.
"The coalition will have a plan to take Australia into the 21st century with a modern, fairer, better tax system," Liberal-National Prime Minister John Howard told reporters.
Howard launched an inquiry into tax reform and promised to present a tax policy before the election due by mid-1999.

He even endorsed the possibility of a goods and services tax (GST), the very measure that whipped up a wave of hostility in 1993 to save the ageing Labor administration of then prime minister Paul Keating, despite near-record unemployment.
Now in opposition, Labor was quick to condemn Howard's backing for a GST, although Opposition Leader Kim Beazley said he would look at the government's proposals when they were finalised.
"A GST kills small business, which is the job-growth centre of business at the moment" he said.
It would also be hard on families, he added.
Critics say the current Australian tax system relies too heavily on income tax. Marginal rates rise rapidly to almost 50 percent, encouraging avoidance.
The maze of indirect taxes applies unevenly on some, but not all, categories of goods. But services are barely taxed at all, even though they constitute an increasing share of national production.

Looking over his shoulder at the conservatives' 1993 poll disaster, Howard successfully campaigned for the 1996 election with a solemn and oft-repeated promise to introduce no GST and indeed no new taxes at all in his first term of office.
But business leaders have continued to press for a GST, keeping the issue on the boil, and they quickly endorsed Howard's strategy on Wednesday.

"His emphasis on a broad-based, simplified indirect tax system...will make an important contribution to a tax system better able to attract investment, create jobs and promote exports," said Mark Paterson, chief executive of the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry.
In fact, Howard did not quite commit himself to a GST.
Rather, he launched the bureaucratic inquiry, said a new indirect tax would have to be considered and reaffirmed his long-standing support for a GST.

"I want to make it very clear to you that I have a strong personal commitment to taxation reform, that I have a very clear view of the directions that I would like to go in reforming the Australian taxation system," he told reporters.
He would not say when the inquiry would report but repeated his commitment to introduce no new tax before the new election.
The government's once commanding lead over the opposition in opinion polls has slipped away this year.
The Reuters Poll Trend, a smoothed average of the polls, shows that if an election were held now the government would survive with a greatly reduced majority.
